durgapuja.title: Durga Puja — The City That Never Sleeps
durgapuja.description: For five days every autumn, Kolkata stops being a city and becomes a festival. Elaborate pandals rise on every street corner, some modelled on palaces, some on entire villages, and the beat of the dhak drums follows you everywhere. The idols of Goddess Durga, caught mid-battle with the demon Mahishasura, are crafted by artisans who spend months on them. We walked from pandal to pandal until dawn, fuelled by street food and endless cups of chai. The final day brings sindoor khela, when married women smear each other in vermilion, and then the emotional immersion of the idols in the Ganga. It is joyful, loud, and deeply moving.

shivtemple.title: 108 Shiva Temples — A Circle of Devotion
shivtemple.description: Rising from the quiet Bengal countryside, the 108 Shiva Temple complex at Kalna is built in two concentric circles, with each small temple housing its own Shiva lingam. Commissioned in the early nineteenth century by the Maharaja of Burdwan, it is as much a feat of geometry as of faith. Walking the circular path in the early morning, with incense in the air and priests beginning their rituals, feels like stepping into a mandala. The temples are modest in size, but their repetition creates a rhythm that is hypnotic. It is a peaceful, little-visited corner of Bengal that rewards slow travellers.

kathgola.title: Kathgola Bagan Bari — A Palace in the Garden
kathgola.description: Tucked away on the banks of the Bhagirathi, Kathgola Bagan Bari is the grand nineteenth-century residence of the Dugar family, wealthy Jain merchants of Murshidabad. The mansion sits within a sprawling garden, and its collection of paintings, furniture and curiosities makes the whole estate feel like a time capsule. A beautiful Jain temple stands within the grounds, and its carved marble is a quiet contrast to the opulence of the main house. Visiting at golden hour, with the light slanting through the old trees, we felt as though the family had only just stepped out. A rare window into the merchant elegance of old Bengal.

krishnachandra.title: Krishna Chandra Temple — Pinnacles of Terracotta
krishnachandra.description: Built in the eighteenth century by the Burdwan royal family, the Krishna Chandra Temple is crowned with twenty-five pinnacles arranged in tiers, a form known as pancha-vimshati ratna. Its walls are covered in terracotta panels that tell stories from the Ramayana and Mahabharata, as well as scenes of village life from centuries ago. Standing close, you can pick out tiny details: warriors, dancers, boats, and animals, all moulded by hand. It is one of Bengal's finest examples of the terracotta tradition and a reminder of how skilled local artisans once were. Come in the morning when the light brings out every carved line.

katramasjid.title: Katra Masjid — Where a Nawab Rests Beneath Your Feet
katramasjid.description: Commissioned in the early 1720s by Murshid Quli Khan, the first Nawab of Bengal, the Katra Masjid was once a great mosque and centre of learning. Its sturdy brick structure is anchored by corner minarets and rows of arched cells where students once studied. The most striking detail is that the Nawab is buried beneath the entrance staircase, so that every worshipper treads over his grave on the way in. The mosque is quiet now, its courtyard open to the sky, but the scale of it hints at the power of Bengal's old capital. A thoughtful, atmospheric stop in Murshidabad.

epidaurus.title: Theatre of Epidaurus — The Perfect Acoustic
epidaurus.description: Built in the fourth century BC within the sanctuary of Asklepios, the god of healing, the Theatre of Epidaurus is often called the best-preserved ancient Greek theatre. Its fan-shaped seating bank holds around fourteen thousand people, and the acoustics are famous: a coin dropped on the central stage can be heard from the very top row. We tested it ourselves, and it is startlingly true. The setting among pine-covered hills adds to the magic. Performances are still staged here in summer, which means the theatre is not a ruin but a living space, still doing the job it was built for.
